title: Swagger UI WebMCP
pitch: If you can Try it out, your agent can too — a Swagger UI plugin that turns any OpenAPI docs page into a live agent interface, using the environment and login you already have open.
about_excerpt: If you can Try it out, your agent can too — a Swagger UI plugin that turns any OpenAPI docs page into a live agent interface, using the environment and login you already have open. Like Comment Story Updates If you can Try it out, your agent can too. Swagger UI WebMCP is a reusable Swagger UI plugin that turns any OpenAPI documentation page into a live, session-scoped agent interface — and splits the decision of what that agent may touch among the four parties who each know something different. The agent calls the API through the exact environment, login, and request pipeline the developer already has open in the page. No AI SDK. No MCP server to install. No bearer token copied anywhere. Live demo: https://openapi-web-mcp.vercel.app Repository: https://github.com/alliecatowo/openapi-web-mcp The problem A developer working against an internal or partner API already has a browser tab where everything is correct: signed in, staging selected in the server dropdown, the right key pasted into Swagger UI's Authorize dialog, and the corporate proxy, CORS rules, and session cookies all working. To let an agent help with that same API, the entire environment has to be rebuilt somewhere else — install or write an MCP server, re-describe the endpoints, copy a bearer token out of the browser into a config file, and keep the two in sync forever. So the agent is useful for writing code about the API and useless for actually driving it. Underneath that is a second problem nobody has a good answer for: once the connector exists, who decides what the agent may touch? Today it is whoever wrote it, once, months ago, holding standing credentials. Audience: developers, QA and support engineers, and solutions/API-partner teams who live in OpenAPI documentation pages every day — and the API publishers who host those pages for them. Every internal and partner API with a Swagger UI docs page is a candidate. The idea: authority splits four ways, and only ever narrows Four parties each hold information the others don't, so each gets exactly the instrument they have the information for: the API publisher knows which endpoints are dangerous, expressed as x-webmcp annotations that travel with the OpenAPI document itself, reviewed and versioned; the page owner knows what this deployment is for, expressed as a webMcp.exposure default and an optional policyResolver; the person at the page knows what is happening right now, expressed as per-operation session locks scoped to this tab only; and the WebMCP client knows what to ask a human, expressed through MCP annotations and structured errors. The rule that makes them compose rather than conflict: every source may only tighten. All of them reduce to a level on the lattice hidden < read < write, the tightest wins, and hidden survives every setting, because refusing exposure is never a privilege escalation. The agent itself does not get a vote — session locks are module state the tools never touch. Why the documentation page is the right place WebMCP's defining property is that the page is the integration: capability lives in the tab, scoped to the session, and dies with it. API docs fit that shape better than almost anything else. The contract already exists and is machine-readable, so tools are derived, not hand-written. The ambient state — selected server, authorized schemes, cookies, interceptors — is simply already true in the tab. Ephemerality is a feature: nobody wants a persistent connector holding standing write access to production. And it generalizes: every Swagger UI page that adds one import becomes an agent surface for whatever API it documents. That surface is not small. swagger-ui-dist alone is pulled from npm roughly 51 million times a month, and Swagger UI is the default, unmodified docs renderer behind FastAPI's /docs route and NestJS's official OpenAPI module — so the install base this plugs into is already deployed, already authenticated, and already pointed at real APIs. (npm registry, 30 days ending 29 Aug 2026; per-package figures in the README.) This is not "write another MCP server" — no standing credentials, no separately maintained tool definitions. And it is not a browser-automation agent clicking through the UI — it calls the API directly through Swagger's own execution pipeline, with a generated tool schema and MCP annotations per operation. What people and agents can do together The human signs in, picks Sandbox, authorizes a scheme in Swagger's own dialog — the agent inherits all of it, live. The person types into the q box of Try it out and stops; the agent reads that value and finishes the call. Every agent execution renders in Swagger UI's own response panel, not a separate agent console. An access control sits next to Try-it-out on every operation: Full access, View only, Read only, Hidden. And the demo API logs whether each write arrived via the agent pipeline or by hand. The thing that was hard before: letting an agent act on a live, authenticated, environment-specific API without provisioning it any standing credentials or infrastructure — and being able to see, constrain, and revoke that in the same place you were already working. The bigger picture The four-way split is in service of something larger than one docs page. It turns an existing, enormous class of page into an agent gateway with no new infrastructure to run or revoke. The per-operation access control doubles as a supervised playground: turn an agent loose on a live API, watch every call land in the same response panel you use yourself, and keep the kill switch one click away. Because agent calls run through Swagger's own execute action — the same code path as Try it out — an agent's call and a human's call are directly comparable, which makes the page a debugging surface. And the mechanism the demo uses to fingerprint agent writes is exported: the plugin's agentExecution primitive is set for the duration of an agent-initiated request and cleared in a finally, so any Swagger UI deployment can read it from its own requestInterceptor and tag agent traffic in its own audit trail. None of that needs different code — it is the same lattice and the same execution path, looked at from four angles. How WebMCP was implemented One import into an existing Swagger UI config is the whole integration. When the browser provides document.modelContext, the plugin enumerates operations from Swagger UI's own resolved spec, resolves local $refs, converts parameters and request bodies into JSON Schema tool inputs, and registers two layers of tools: five stable core tools plus one direct tool per exposed operation, capped at 64 with graceful fallback to discovery and generic execution. The cap is enforced everywhere a tool name is advertised, so search and get can never name a tool that was not registered. Tools can never name a URL. A call resolves against the currently selected Swagger server and does not build its own fetch client — arguments are written into the Swagger
video_transcript_excerpt: SwaggerUI, webMCP, a plugin that turns any OpenAPI documentation page into an agent interface. The problem, a developer already has a tab where they're signed in on the right environment with the right key. To let an agent help, all of that has to be rebuilt somewhere else. Here's how it's implemented. One import into an existing slider config registers tools on document.model context compiled from the OpenAPI document this page just loaded. Five core tools plus one per operation. Nothing was installed. No MCP server, no token pasted anywhere. Load a different document and the whole tool set is re-derived. Same fields, same session, no copies. I typed half a thought into try it out and stopped. The agent reads what's on screen, finishes the call, and submits it through Swagger's own pipeline. And the result lands in Swagger's own response panel where I'd look for my own. Seeing isn't calling. The document says this endpoint needs bearer authorization and nobody's authorized yet. So, the agent can see it and say exactly what it needs, but the call is refused. I authorize in the normal Swagger dialog, the same one I'd use myself. The agent's next call follows the page's live state. No re-registration, no second setup. This is the control I care most about. I don't run the billing server, so I can't annotate it, but I can still narrow what the agent may touch. Right now from the docs page. Read only lets reads through and denies rights. Hidden removes the operation from the agent's world entirely. Locks only ever tighten what the document allows. The agent has no tool that can change them, and a reload resets everything. I'm never restricted. Watch, it still works by hand. This is why it belongs in the page. I change the environment by hand. The agent's tools didn't change and didn't need to. They read the page's current selection at call time. That's the WebMCP argument. The capability is the tab, and it dies with the tab. Multi-step work runs as one plan, checked whole before anything executes. If one step isn't allowed, nothing runs. And every agent call leaves receipts in the page, in Swagger's own panels, and server-side where the API logs which pipeline served it. Agent writes versus mine. Honestly, that's an audit hint, not identity proof. The OpenAPI document was already the contract. WebMCP lets the live documentation page become the connector, with the person holding the locks sharing the very same fields and reading the receipts.

live_observation.first_impression: Swagger UI WebMCP presents OpenAPI documents and per-operation agent-access controls.
live_observation.after_state: Operation controls became visible; no authenticated execution attempted.
live_observation.notes: Clearly demonstrates OpenAPI operations as agent-configurable tools.
